newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMPOVERISHED BULGARIANS PESSIMISTIC ON ECONOMY.
newsitem.headline: IMPOVERISHED BULGARIANS PESSIMISTIC ON ECONOMY.

text.p: Bulgarians are pessimistic about the country's economic prospects and their own living standards this year, a survey conducted by the National Statistics Institute (NSI) showed.

"Pessimism dominates all consumers forecasts and their confidence index, being eroded by economic hardship, has fallen threefold in two years," head of NSI Business Statistics Department Teofana Genova told a news conference on Thursday.
Some 90 percent of 1,156 people surveyed said their financial state grew worse in the past year and 83 percent expect inflation to rise this year.

Forty-eight percent of those interviewed said they could hardly make ends meet in their family budget, every fourth Bulgarian is in debt and 71 percent have postponed indefinitely the purchase of goods other than food and clothing, such as cars, television sets or washing machines.
But 3.4 percent are optimistic about their finances this year and 14 percent of the people surveyed expect them to remain the same.
Only three percent say their financial state has improved and seven percent say it has remained unchanged in the past year, the survey showed.
The NSI said incomes had fallen by 21 percent in the past year. The highest state enterprise wage was that of dockworkers, 60,000 levs, while the average state wage was 20,000 levs.

The consumer confidence index (CCI), used by international statistics agencies to describe financial wellbeing expectations of households based on the country's general economic performance has fallen from minus 24 percent in 1995 to minus 69.2 percent this year, said Genova.
Delayed reform over the past seven years, mismanagement by the previous Socialist administration and persistent asset stripping of banks and factories left the country in disarray.

The lev currency has fallen by some 300 percent against the dollar since the beginning of the year and economists see February inflation at around 100 percent. Monthly inflation last month was 44 percent.

In the beginning of February, after month-long mass protests President Petar Stoyanov mediated a deal providing for an early general election on April 19, dissolved parliament and named a caretaker cabinet.

The caretaker cabinet may reach a preliminary funding agreement with the International Monetary Fund to help stabilise the economy and repay foreign debts, Finance Minister Svetoslav Gavriiski said on Wednesday.

Businessmen interviewed by the NSI saw Bulgaria's business climate worsening and expected transport and retail trade to shrink further. They attribute the insecure economic environment to insolvency of companies and banks narrowing markets and shrinking demand, said the NSI. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
